Question six. What is the Strategy pattern? It puts interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, and lets the caller pick one at runtime, instead of a sprawling if-else. A shipment holds a pricing strategy and asks it for the cost. For a parcel weighing three, the flat rate says five. Pricing by weight, at two a unit, says six. A third rule, free above a weight of ten, is a new class. The shipment isn't edited: that's open-closed. With only one rule, though, the interface is just indirection. A plain function does the job until a second rule really arrives.

Question seven. What is the Observer pattern? A one-to-many dependency: when a subject changes state, it notifies every observer that registered. An order is placed. The email, the stock count and the analytics have each subscribed, and each one hears about it. The order doesn't know their types, so a fourth, for loyalty points, joins without an edit to the order. It underpins event systems, UI data binding, and publish-subscribe. The cost is indirection. Reading the checkout no longer tells you what happens after an order; you have to go and find who subscribed.

Question eight. When does a design pattern become over-engineering? When it adds indirection without a need to match. A factory for a class that will only ever have one implementation. A strategy interface with one strategy. An observer with one hard-coded listener. Each is abstraction you have to read through, for flexibility nobody uses. Patterns solve variation you expect. Added speculatively, they break yag-nee: you aren't gonna need it. So in an interview, name the trigger rather than the pattern. The second shipping rule is the day the strategy earns its interface. Reach for a pattern when the duplication, or the pressure to change, is real.
